explanations: terra: Each tribe knows its drinking place when water is brought from the rock, a collective provision divided without becoming one person's enclosed supply.
terra: Believers are أَشَدُّ حُبًّا لِّلَّهِ; the same intensity language redirects severe love from wealth to God.
terra: Believers eat from wholesome provision and give thanks, joining clean source, shared food ethics, and the gratitude attached to the section's great pots.

luna: The section's root حبّ depicts attachment to wealth; this ayah makes giving wealth “عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ” part of righteousness, so love need not end in hoarding. The phrase can retain the sense of giving while the wealth is loved. | terra: Righteousness includes giving wealth عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ to relatives and vulnerable people, the same love-of-property tension resolved by release.

luna: The section explicitly identifies its dictionary sense of الخير as wealth; this testamentary ayah uses “خَيْرًا” for what a person leaves and directs a bequest to parents and relatives. | terra: إِن تَرَكَ خَيْرًا uses khayr for property left behind and orders a bequest to parents and relatives, confirming the section's wealth sense while directing it into shares.
terra: Feeding a poor person is the compensating act for one unable to fast, another concrete transfer of one's food into a vulnerable person's portion.

luna: The section calls good wealth that acquired from a praiseworthy way; this boundary forbids consuming one another's wealth unjustly (“بِالْبَاطِلِ”), distinguishing legitimate provision from wrongful gain. | terra: The ban on consuming one another's property falsely sets the negative boundary around the section's “good” wealth gathered from a praiseworthy source.

luna: The section identifies “خَيْر” as wealth; in this answer about what to spend, “مِنْ خَيْرٍ” is directed to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and travelers. | terra: The answer about what khayr is spent names parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and the traveler, converting “good” property into a widening table of beneficiaries.
terra: The warning that one may love a thing while it is bad directly limits the source definition of love as desiring what one sees or supposes to be good.
terra: One ayah joins wine, gambling, and the answer قُلِ ٱلْعَفْوَ about what to spend; it brings together the section's drinking cup, gambling lots, and the surplus that should leave the hand.
terra: The instruction that mixing life or property with orphans makes them brothers supplies a communal alternative to consuming orphan wealth into one's own store.

terra: The good loan releases wealth while God both constricts and expands provision; the ayah redirects the imagery of contraction and opening from the human fist to divine measure and multiplication.

luna: The section shows wealth collected into a closed reserve; this parable pictures wealth spent for God as a grain multiplying into many ears, a different kind of increase than hoarding. | terra: Wealth spent in God's way is likened to a seed multiplying into many grains, answering the collector's desire for increase with abundance produced by release.

luna: The section says its dictionary sense of الخير is substantial wealth from a good source; this command to spend from good earnings (“مِن طَيِّبَاتِ مَا كَسَبْتُمْ”) forbids selecting the bad for others. | terra: The command to spend from the good things one has earned, not deliberately offer the defective, grounds the section's claim that wealth called khayr comes by a praised and wholesome route.

luna: This ayah identifies fear of poverty as a force against spending (“الشَّيْطَانُ يَعِدُكُمُ الْفَقْرَ”) and sets God's promise of bounty against it, sharpening the section's image of holding wealth from fear. | terra: Satan promises poverty while God promises bounty; this identifies the fear that makes the imagined owner of even divine treasuries clutch them.
terra: Whatever khayr people spend returns fully to them, making the same word the object of outward giving rather than inward attachment.

luna: The section names الخير as wealth and also as generosity; for a debtor in hardship this ayah says to grant time, and that remitting the debt as charity is better (“وَأَن تَصَدَّقُوا خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ”).

terra: Love of desired things is adorned through amassed gold and silver, fine horses, cattle, and fields; it expands the section's desire for perceived good into a full inventory of attachable wealth.
terra: Whether people hide what is in their breasts or disclose it, God knows it; this states the knowledge that makes the final exposure unavoidable.
terra: The guardians cast their pens to decide who will care for Mary, another Qur'anic lot scene that shows selection by cast objects outside gambling.

luna: The section's root حبّ joins love to what one takes for good; “مِمَّا تُحِبُّونَ” says righteousness is not reached until some of what one loves is spent. | terra: One cannot attain true goodness until spending from what one loves; the ayah turns the section's love of khayr into the test of letting the loved thing go.
terra: Holding together to God's rope جَمِيعًا and refusing division gives the gathering root a communal direction opposite to gathering wealth into one fist.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss of شديد is بخيل; those who withhold (“بَخِلُوا”) what God gave will be made to wear it as a collar (“سَيُطَوَّقُونَ”), turning stinginess into a bodily bond. | terra: What people withhold will be put around their necks on Resurrection, so the kept wealth becomes the bodily bond imagined by the section; the ayah also ends with God's being خَبِيرٌ.

luna: The section's shared table includes the orphan; this command requires handing orphans their property and forbids consuming it or exchanging the good for the bad (“وَلَا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوَالَهُمْ”). | terra: The command to return orphans' property and not consume it into one's own wealth marks the boundary against swelling one store by swallowing another's share.

terra: Property is called a means of support, yet guardians must provide food and clothing from it for dependents; the store exists to sustain a household rather than merely remain in the guardian's fist.

luna: This ayah bounds a guardian's use of orphan wealth: the rich must refrain from consuming it, while a poor guardian may take only fairly; the wealth is entrusted, not a private hoard. | terra: A rich guardian must abstain from an orphan's property, a needy one may take fairly, and matured property must be handed over, setting exact limits against absorbing another's share.

luna: The section's common pot and divided portions oppose taking all for oneself; this ayah assigns a prescribed share in inheritance to both men and women, whether the estate is small or large. | terra: Men and women alike receive assigned shares from what parents and relatives leave, a legal form of the section's one accumulation being divided among participants.

luna: At the division of an inheritance, this ayah directs that attending relatives, orphans, and the poor be given something from it; it makes the section's shared provision concrete at an estate. | terra: When relatives, orphans, and the poor attend an estate's division, they are to be provided from it; the ayah stages wealth being apportioned around those present instead of consumed alone.

luna: Where the section opposes solitary consumption and withholding, this ayah warns that consuming orphan property unjustly is like eating fire (“أَمْوَالَ الْيَتَامَىٰ ظُلْمًا”). | terra: Those who consume orphans' property unjustly only consume fire into their bellies; wrongful solitary eating is turned back bodily on the eater.

luna: The section's dictionary form describes wealth gathered by a praiseworthy means; this ayah prohibits wrongful consumption and allows trade by mutual consent (“تِجَارَةً عَن تَرَاضٍ”), clarifying that source. | terra: The ayah forbids consuming one another's wealth wrongfully and allows mutually agreed trade, specifying a clean route by which property may enter the hand.
terra: Kindness is commanded toward the poor, nearby companion, traveler, and those under one's authority, directly reversing the kenud who eats alone, strikes his servant, and withholds help.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss of شديد is بخيل; this ayah describes misers (“يَبْخَلُونَ”) who urge others to be miserly and conceal God's bounty (“وَيَكْتُمُونَ مَا آتَاهُمُ اللَّهُ”). | terra: Those who are miserly, command miserliness, and conceal God's bounty reproduce the section's store both as a shut hand and as hidden provision.

luna: The section's dictionary sense of قَدْح includes an arrow used in maysir; this ayah prohibits using divining arrows (“بِالْأَزْلَامِ”), setting a boundary around taking shares by lot. | terra: The prohibition of dividing or seeking a decision by arrows, وَأَن تَسْتَقْسِمُوا بِٱلْأَزْلَامِ, directly activates the section's lots used to allot portions, while distinguishing a forbidden rite.

terra: The accusation that God's hand is bound is rejected with بَلْ يَدَاهُ مَبْسُوطَتَانِ يُنفِقُ كَيْفَ يَشَاءُ; bound and outspread hands make the section's withholding-versus-giving contrast explicit.
terra: Eating what God has provided as lawful and wholesome corresponds to the section's requirement that property called khayr come from a clean source.
terra: The expiation feeds ten poor people from the ordinary food of one's household, a concrete table where a household's provision is measured into shared portions.

luna: The section's arrow-and-share dictionary image meets the Qur'an's condemnation of maysir and arrows (“الْمَيْسِرُ وَالْأَزْلَامُ”); this is a contrary form of distributing a portion, not a communal meal. | terra: Wine, gambling, sacrificial stones, and divining arrows are named together; this is the Qur'anic setting for the section's drinking vessel and gaming arrows.
terra: Wine and gambling create hostility and obstruct remembrance and prayer, stating what the section's cup and gaming arrows do when their social sharing is corrupted.
terra: Sea catch and its food are made provision for people and travelers, giving the section's traveler-meal detail a direct Qur'anic source of food.

luna: The section's meal and divided portions meet the harvest scene: eat the fruit when it bears and give its due on harvest day (“وَآتُوا حَقَّهُ يَوْمَ حَصَادِهِ”), without excess. | terra: At harvest the eater must give its due and not be excessive, an agricultural instance of bounty entering a common claim instead of a private heap.
terra: The person who أَخْلَدَ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ and followed desire supplies a human analogue to the section's animal that plants itself and will not move.
terra: The repeated warning that wealth and children are a trial marks possessions as a test of the holder rather than an uncomplicated good.

luna: This ayah assigns defined shares from gathered spoils to relatives, orphans, poor people, and travelers; its allocation of a common acquisition parallels the section's divided portions and shared food.
terra: Accumulated wealth, feared-for trade, and pleasing dwellings are tested by whether they are more beloved than God and His cause, clarifying when property-love becomes captivity.

luna: The section's miser stores what could have become shared food; this ayah names those who hoard gold and silver (“يَكْنِزُونَ الذَّهَبَ وَالْفِضَّةَ”) and do not spend it for God. | terra: The ayah joins consuming people's wealth wrongfully to hoarding gold and silver and not spending it, uniting bad source, solitary consumption, and the closed store.

luna: The next ayah gives the hoard a bodily end: the gold and silver become the heated metal that brands their foreheads, sides, and backs, reversing secure storage into punishment. | terra: The hoarded metal is heated and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs; what the hand stored is materially turned upon the body of its keeper.
terra: When called to go forth, people become heavy toward the earth and accept worldly life over the Hereafter; attachment is rendered as arrested motion.
terra: Wealth and children are not to inspire admiration because they may become a means of punishment, challenging the assumption that abundant possessions deserve the name good.
terra: Obligatory alms are apportioned among named recipients including the poor, captives, debtors, and traveler, a formal division of the stored wealth into communal shares.

luna: The section's dictionary definition of the fist uses تقبضها (closing the palm); this ayah says hypocrites “يَقْبِضُونَ أَيْدِيَهُمْ,” physically closing their hands and withholding, a direct opposite to the shared table. | terra: وَيَقْبِضُونَ أَيْدِيَهُمْ makes refusal to give visible as hands drawn shut, nearly the section's exact bodily picture of miserliness.

luna: This ayah gives the promise that precedes 9:76: if given bounty, they will give charity; 9:76 then shows the promise reversed once provision arrives. | terra: A person promises that if God gives from His bounty he will give charity and be righteous, setting the promised opening of the hand that 9:76 reverses.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss of شديد is بخيل; when these people receive bounty, they “بَخِلُوا بِهِ” and turn away, making the closed hand a response to provision. | terra: Once bounty is given, the recipients become miserly with it and turn away, a compact narrative of good-seeming wealth fastening and closing its new owner.

luna: After the withholding in 9:76, this ayah says hypocrisy is left in their hearts (“نِفَاقًا فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ”) until they meet God; it gives the inward consequence beside the section's gathered chest.
terra: Taking charity from their wealth purifies and increases them, making release from the store the means of cleansing the possessor rather than diminishing him.

luna: The section's hidden chest is made explicit here: people fold their breasts (“يَثْنُونَ صُدُورَهُمْ”) to conceal, while God knows what they hide and reveal. | terra: People fold their breasts to hide, yet God knows what they conceal and disclose; it supplies the hiding gesture before the section's final uncovering.

luna: A second telling of Abraham's guest scene serves a roasted calf (“بِعِجْلٍ حَنِيذٍ”); it recalls the section's dictionary form for a meal prepared for a traveler, though the Qur'an calls these guests rather than travelers. | terra: Abraham promptly brings a roasted calf to visiting messengers, a Qur'anic instance of an animal prepared as food for arriving travelers rather than retained for oneself.
terra: Abraham notices that the visitors' hands do not reach the offered calf; the same visible relation of hand to common food here signals angelic guests, not miserliness.
terra: Full measure and weight are commanded and people must not be deprived of their goods, setting fairness around the apportioning action evoked by the common pot and lots.
terra: Joseph places the drinking vessel in his brother's grain bag during a scene of measured provisions, bringing the section's cup into an actual distribution of food stores.
terra: Shackles on necks repeat the yoke object behind the section's dictionary image, though the ayah does not connect that restraint to property or withheld food.
terra: Those who prefer worldly life over the Hereafter make attachment a deliberate ordering of loves, of which love of wealth is the section's bodily example.
terra: What is with people perishes while what is with God remains, directly overturning the hoarder's hope that retained wealth can make him permanent.
terra: Preferring worldly life over the Hereafter explains disbelief as misplaced love, parallel to the section's good-seeming property fixing desire in place.
terra: A secure town receives abundant provision from every place but is ungrateful for God's favors, joining plentiful food to the kenud response and to provision withdrawn.
terra: Lawful, wholesome provision is to be eaten with gratitude, joining clean source, food, and the gratitude attached to the great pots in 34:13.

luna: The section binds the hand and later gathers what is inside; this ayah binds each person's record to their neck and brings it out open (“كِتَابًا يَلْقَاهُ مَنشُورًا”), making the bodily bond answerable at judgment.
luna: After the open record in 17:13, this ayah commands each person to read their own book (“اقْرَأْ كِتَابَكَ”); it makes the disclosure personal, beside the section's account of inner contents.
luna: The hand image in 17:29 belongs to a passage about giving: this ayah assigns relatives, the needy, and travelers their due and warns against waste, setting both sides of the boundary.
luna: Between the due to others in 17:26 and the bound hand in 17:29, this ayah warns that spendthrifts are brothers of devils; the shared meal must not become excess.

luna: Between giving others their due in 17:26 and the bound hand in 17:29, this ayah says that if one must turn a needy petitioner away while awaiting God's bounty, one should still speak gently; it separates inability to give from hardness.

luna: The section's dictionary reading of root ش د د is binding tightly, and its fist is gathered shut; this command names a hand bound to the neck (“مَغْلُولَةً إِلَىٰ عُنُقِكَ”), the bodily image of stinginess. | terra: The command not to make one's hand مَغْلُولَةً إِلَىٰ عُنُقِكَ gives the section's clenched hand and neck-bound yoke their explicit Qur'anic moral image.

luna: The section's wording رَبّ and خَبِير at 100:6,11 recurs here: after the hand-bound command in 17:29, this ayah says the Lord expands and restricts provision (“يَبْسُطُ الرِّزْقَ ... وَيَقْدِرُ”) and is fully aware of servants. | terra: After the bound-hand warning, the Lord expands or measures provision and is خَبِيرًا بَصِيرًا of His servants; it places human clenching under divine apportionment and knowledge.

luna: The section's tight hand is stated directly: people would hold back from spending (“لَأَمْسَكْتُمْ”) for fear of depletion, and the ayah calls the human being “قَتُورًا”. | terra: Humans would clutch even the treasuries of the Lord's mercy from fear of spending; this states the fear inside the section's tight hand and calls humanity قَتُورًا.
terra: The sleepers send one member with their silver to seek the purest food and bring provision back to the group, closely matching jointly purchased wholesome food shared from one common store.
terra: The garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and a stronger following, establishing the possessive confidence whose collapse is shown in his palms at 18:42.
terra: He supposes his garden will not perish and expects an even better return, echoing the illusion that wealth secures permanence.
terra: After the garden's wealth is ruined, its owner turns his palms over what he spent; the once-secure property returns as an anguished hand-image.

luna: The section's fixation on “خَيْر” as property is bounded here: wealth and children are adornment of worldly life, while enduring good deeds (“وَالْبَاقِيَاتُ الصَّالِحَاتُ”) are better and last. | terra: Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while lasting good deeds are better with the Lord; this separates possessed “good” from what actually remains.

luna: Under the wall of two orphans is a hidden treasure (“كَنزٌ لَّهُمَا”), preserved for them by their righteous father; the stored wealth is a deliberate provision for others, opposite the section's self-hoarder.
terra: God gathers all people together at the final blast, reversing the collector's agency: the one who gathered property becomes part of the gathered multitude.
terra: Worldly splendor is a test, while the Lord's provision is better and more lasting; apparent property-khayr is measured against enduring provision.

luna: The section's feast for an arriving traveler has a close ritual counterpart: this ayah tells pilgrims to eat sacrificial livestock and feed the distressed poor. | terra: Pilgrims eat from sacrificial livestock and feed the distressed poor, another direct Qur'anic division of slaughtered animal food.

luna: The section gathers the shared table around a large pot and divided meat; here sacrificed camels provide food to eat and to give to the needy, joining provision to sharing. | terra: The shared meat of sacrificial camels, eaten and fed to others, is the Qur'anic opposite of the section's animal wealth and food kept by one eater.
terra: Neither sacrificial meat nor blood reaches God, but mindfulness does; it prevents the shared slaughter image from being mistaken for mere material offering.
terra: Messengers are commanded to eat wholesome things and act rightly, reinforcing the section's link between food from a clean source and praiseworthy action.
terra: The question asks whether extended wealth and children are being mistaken for benefits, directly testing the section's equation of abundant property with perceived khayr.
terra: The answer says they do not understand that wealth and children are not necessarily good things being hastened to them, correcting the owner's judgment of what counts as khayr.
terra: Owners are commanded to contract with enslaved people seeking freedom and give them from God's wealth, directly reversing the section's master who harms his servant and withholds aid.
terra: The explicit permission to eat جَمِيعًا أَوْ أَشْتَاتًا supplies the boundary between eating together and separately that the kenud portrait turns into a moral contrast.

luna: The section opposes a fist that will not open with a common table; this ayah places spending between waste and miserliness (“لَمْ يُسْرِفُوا وَلَمْ يَقْتُرُوا”), showing the measured boundary. | terra: The servants of the Merciful spend neither wastefully nor stingily but hold a just middle, supplying the boundary beyond both the tied hand and reckless dispersal.
terra: On the final day neither wealth nor children benefit, removing the collector's outward assets before 26:89 identifies the inward possession that matters.
terra: Only the one who comes with a sound heart succeeds, placing the disclosed condition of the chest where wealth fails in 26:88.
terra: The she-camel has one drinking share and the people another on a known day, pairing an animal with an explicit rule of communal apportionment.

luna: The section's wording about collected chest-contents and the Lord as خبير points to what is hidden inside; this ayah specifies that he knows what their breasts conceal (“مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ”) and disclose.

terra: Moses, a displaced traveler after helping others at the well, declares himself in need of whatever khayr God sends, allowing khayr to be heard as needed provision rather than a possessed store.
terra: One of the women invites Moses so her father may reward his help, moving the needy traveler of 28:24 toward a host household and lawful recompense.
terra: Worldly possessions are temporary enjoyment and adornment, whereas what is with God is better and more lasting, correcting attachment's estimate of retained goods.
luna: This repeated formulation says the Lord knows what breasts conceal and reveal (“مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ”); it parallels the section's collected contents of the chest and divine knowledge.

luna: Qarun's treasuries (“مِنَ الْكُنُوزِ”) and keys too heavy for a strong band of men give a concrete image of abundance accumulated, the section's “خَيْر” as much wealth turned into a burden. | terra: Qarun's treasure keys burden a strong company, giving abundant wealth literal weight and turning “much property” into something that bears down on bodies.

luna: Beside Qarun's treasure, this ayah directs him to seek the Hereafter with what God gave, do good as God has done good, and not spread corruption: wealth is judged by its use. | terra: Qarun is told to seek the final abode with what God gave him and to do good, redirecting a great store toward its proper end.

luna: Qarun appears in full ornament before those who covet his worldly display; this gives a scene of wealth drawing desire, like the section's love that fixes on property. | terra: Those desiring worldly life wish for wealth like Qarun's, exposing love as wanting what appears good and splendid.
terra: Those given knowledge answer that God's reward is better, correcting the spectators' estimate of Qarun's apparent khayr.

luna: The earth swallows Qarun and his house, and no group can rescue him; the fate reverses the security implied by hoarded treasure. | terra: Qarun and his dwelling are swallowed, and no company or self-help can save him; the great store and social strength of 28:76 prove unable to hold their owner up.

luna: After Qarun's fall, those who wanted his position recognize that provision is expanded or restricted by God (“يَبْسُطُ الرِّزْقَ ... وَيَقْدِرُ”), not secured by wealth. | terra: After Qarun's fall, his former admirers recognize that God expands and restricts provision and that unbelievers do not prosper, correcting their previous desire for his store.
terra: Giving the relative, poor person, and traveler their due repeats the distribution pattern of the section's shared food and returning guest.
terra: Charity given seeking God's favor is what truly multiplies, relocating increase from the counted private store to the gift.

luna: The section's dictionary form for a great communal cauldron meets the Qur'an's “قُدُورٍ رَّاسِيَاتٍ” (fixed cauldrons); the same ayah asks David's household for grateful work, turning abundance into a received trust. | terra: Davud's household has basin-sized dishes and fixed great cooking pots, then is commanded to work in gratitude; this is the section's large common cauldron set against the ungrateful solitary eater.
terra: A prosperous people are told to eat their Lord's provision and thank Him, giving the section's large pot its civic form: abundant food received together in gratitude.
terra: The good land loses its abundance because of ingratitude, showing what follows when provision meets the kenud response rather than the gratitude commanded in 34:15.
terra: Shackles placed on unbelievers' necks provide another literal instance of the bound-neck object; its connection to the section is visual rather than economic.
terra: God replaces whatever is spent, answering the fear of depletion that tightens the hoarder's hand.
terra: Shackles are put on necks up to the chins; this supplies the literal neck-yoke object from which the section builds its bound-hand picture, though wealth is not at issue here.
terra: When told to spend from God's provision, the disbelievers ask why they should feed someone God could feed; the objection voices the refusal behind the section's withheld pot.
terra: A cup from a flowing drink is passed around among the purified servants, matching the section's drinking vessel as a shared rather than hoarded object.
terra: Jonah casts lots and is selected, a non-gambling Qur'anic use of lots that clarifies the allotment mechanism behind the section's gaming arrows.

terra: Solomon says أَحْبَبْتُ حُبَّ ٱلْخَيْرِ of fine horses when they distract him from remembrance; it is the closest other joining of love, khayr understood as valuable animals, and binding attachment.
luna: The section says what is in the chests is gathered and the Lord is “خبير”; this ayah names what God knows there: “وَمَا تُخْفِي الصُّدُورُ,” what breasts conceal.
terra: Shackles on necks and chains stage the bodily restraint named in the section's dictionary image, in a punishment rather than a wealth context.
terra: The human being never tires of asking for khayr, showing desire's persistent reach toward what it perceives as good even before possession turns into withholding.

terra: Had provision been expanded without measure, people would transgress; God sends it in due measure, explaining why abundance is not simply khayr and placing the human hoard under divine apportionment.
terra: Whatever people are given is temporary worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and lasting, the same boundary between possession and true khayr.
terra: Golden plates and cups are circulated among the people of Paradise; precious vessels move through a company instead of becoming a private sealed store.
terra: فَشُدُّوا ٱلْوَثَاقَ uses the section's sh-d-d root in its literal binding sense, making the semantic route from tight fastening to a figuratively tight owner visible.

terra: The ayah says that if people were pressed for their wealth they would become miserly and their hidden rancor would be brought out, joining the wealth test to the section's exposure of what chests contain.
terra: Whoever is miserly is miserly only against himself; this makes the section's turn of the hoard back upon the hoarder explicit.

terra: The sacrificial animals are held back from reaching their place; this may faintly recall the section's immobile camel, but here the beasts are externally prevented rather than stubbornly attached.
terra: A right in their wealth for the asker and deprived turns private property into an acknowledged common claim, matching the section's portions drawn from one store.

luna: The section's dictionary sense of نقيعة is food made for a traveler; Abraham's honored guests receive a fat calf (“بِعِجْلٍ سَمِينٍ”), a specific meal prepared for arrivals. Neighbor 51:27 shows him bring it near and invite them to eat. | terra: Abraham goes quietly to his household and brings a fat calf, supplying the prepared animal in the section's traveler-feast image; 51:27 shows it offered.

luna: The section's traveler's meal is echoed when Abraham brings food close to his arriving guests and asks them to eat (“فَقَرَّبَهُۥٓ إِلَيْهِمْ”); 51:26 identifies it as a fat calf. | terra: He places the calf near the guests and asks why they do not eat, completing the act of presenting food to arrivals begun in 51:26.
terra: The inhabitants pass a cup among themselves, a communal use of the vessel derived in the section from qadh.
terra: Water is divided between the people and the she-camel, each turn attended in order; it is a non-gambling scene of a common resource allotted into known shares.
terra: Serving youths circulate cups, pitchers, and a goblet from a flowing drink, another shared-table realization of the section's secondary drinking-vessel sense.
terra: People are told to spend from property over which they have only been made successors, weakening the absolute ownership imagined by the clenched hand.
terra: Worldly life includes boastful rivalry in wealth and children, then is likened to vegetation that dries and crumbles; the hoard's apparent increase is placed inside a passing cycle.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss of شديد is بخيل; this ayah repeats that miserly word (“يَبْخَلُونَ”) and adds urging others to be miserly, extending the closed hand to a community. | terra: Those who are miserly and command others to be miserly extend the clenched hand into a social norm rather than an isolated vice.
terra: Feeding sixty poor people is required when emancipation and fasting are impossible, turning atonement into a deliberately large communal provision.

luna: On the day all are raised, God informs them of what they did, having counted it while they forgot (“أَحْصَاهُ اللَّهُ وَنَسُوهُ”); divine accounting reverses the section's obsessive counting of wealth.

luna: This ayah distributes communal wealth to relatives, orphans, poor people, and travelers so it does not merely circulate among the rich (“كَيْ لَا يَكُونَ دُولَةً بَيْنَ الْأَغْنِيَاءِ”); it sets the section's shared-pot image against concentrated ownership. | terra: The distribution rule is expressly so wealth does not merely circulate among the rich, a public counterpart to the section's pot whose contents are apportioned rather than enclosed.

luna: The section's dictionary image of the Kenud is one who eats alone and withholds help; the hosts here give others priority even when they themselves need the food, and are guarded from “شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ”. | terra: The hosts feel no need in their breasts for what others receive, prefer others despite need, and are protected from inner greed; every element reverses the clenched chest and solitary meal.
terra: At the Friday gathering, believers leave trade for remembrance; communal jamʿ therefore interrupts commercial attachment rather than serving it.

terra: The command not to spend on those with the Messenger until they disperse is an attempt to break a community by closing provision; the ayah answers that heaven's and earth's treasuries belong to God.

luna: This warning says wealth and children must not distract from remembrance (“لَا تُلْهِكُمْ أَمْوَالُكُمْ”); 63:10 then tells people to spend before death, making the danger of fixation concrete. | terra: The warning not to let wealth and children distract from God's remembrance sets the boundary that Solomon's حب الخير and the section's wealth-love approach.

luna: This ayah urges spending from God's provision before death arrives (“وَأَنفِقُوا مِمَّا رَزَقْنَاكُم”), the available moment for loosening the section's closed hand; 63:11 closes off delay. | terra: Spend from provision before death comes, when the hoarder will wish for delay to give charity; release must precede the grave-opening horizon of surah 100.
luna: This ayah states that no soul is delayed when its term comes (“وَلَن يُؤَخِّرَ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا”); it completes 63:10's urgency to give before death.
terra: God knows what people conceal, disclose, and hold within breasts; in the same surah, 64:9 names the Day of Gathering when this knowledge governs judgment.
terra: The Day of Gathering places all private accumulations inside God's final assembly and judgment, the horizon of the section's exposed chests.
terra: Wealth and children are described as a trial immediately before the command to spend and guard against inner greed in 64:16.

luna: The section shows the fist closed around wealth; this command couples spending from what God provided with protection from the soul's greed (“شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ”), the reverse movement of the hand. | terra: The command to spend what is good for oneself ends by naming protection from the self's شُحّ as the route to success, the explicit cure for the section's inner grip.
terra: The question asks who could provide if God withheld His provision, exposing the human withholder's dependence on a provision he never controlled.
terra: The garden owners resolve that no poor person will enter upon them that day, turning abundance into a deliberately closed harvest.
terra: They set out believing themselves able to withhold the produce, exposing the intention that 68:24 directs against the poor.
terra: When the owners confront their ruined garden they say they have been deprived, turning their plan to deprive the poor in 68:24 into deprivation of themselves.
terra: The chained offender says that his wealth did not avail him, the confessed collapse of the security imagined by the collector before the binding and withheld-food sequence.
terra: The order to seize and shackle the offender gives a literal bond to the section's moral yoke; 69:34 later identifies refusal to urge feeding the poor.
terra: The offender is inserted into a long chain, intensifying the bodily binding whose ethical cause includes the withheld meal in 69:34.
terra: Failure to believe in God stands beside failure to urge feeding the poor in 69:34 and explains why the binding punishment of 69:30-32 is more than an isolated food offense.
luna: The section's Kenud withholds aid; this ayah gives the specific failure, not urging the feeding of the poor (“لَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ”).
terra: The one who would not urge feeding the poor has no food except foul discharge, a punitive reversal of the meal he refused to open to another.
terra: This ayah identifies the subject of the later call as the Blaze, supplying the fire whose calling action in 70:17 reaches the collector of 70:18.
terra: The blaze calls the one who turned his back; 70:18 immediately identifies him as the person who gathered and stored, making hoarding the figure summoned by the fire.

luna: The section's dictionary sense of جمع is drawing parts together; “وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ” describes the person who gathers wealth and keeps it stored away, the same closed-fist action. | terra: وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ names both gathering and putting away in a container, the precise hoarding action opposed to the section's common pot.

luna: This ayah describes the restless human (“هَلُوعًا”) whose pattern the next two verses specify: when hardship touches him he panics (70:20), but when good touches him he withholds (70:21); the section focuses on that latter response.

luna: This is the other half of the pattern surrounding the section's cited 70:21: at hardship the human is “جَزُوعًا,” while 70:21 says he withholds when good reaches him. It distinguishes panic from the miser's response to having provision.

luna: The section explicitly notes that here “الْخَيْرُ” is wealth and that the human is miserly; “وَإِذَا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعًا” puts good and withholding together. | terra: When al-khayr touches the human being, he becomes مَنُوعًا; the same human-and-khayr pairing explains the love of wealth in 100:8 as withholding.

luna: The section's common meal answers the hoarder's withholding; this passage says the just have a known right in their wealth (“فِي أَمْوَالِهِمْ حَقٌّ مَّعْلُومٌ”), which 70:25 identifies for the asker and deprived person. | terra: The exception to withholding has a مَالِهِمْ حَقٌّ مَّعْلُومٌ, a known share within wealth; 70:25 names those for whom that share is kept open.

luna: This ayah names the recipients of the known wealth-right from 70:24, “لِلسَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ”; it makes the section's shared provision concrete. | terra: The known portion in 70:24 belongs to the petitioner and deprived person, specifying the recipients excluded by the hoarder's closed hand.
terra: Whatever khayr people send ahead for themselves will be found with God as better and greater in reward, presenting the enduring deposit opposed to counted property.
terra: The condemned man is given extended wealth, establishing the abundance that 74:15 says still fails to satisfy him.
terra: ثُمَّ يَطْمَعُ أَنْ أَزِيدَ shows attachment persisting after ample wealth: possession does not loosen desire but asks for more.
terra: The people of the Fire confess that they did not feed the poor, making exclusion from the meal a stated cause of their end.
terra: The people are likened to startled donkeys in flight; this may faintly extend the section's contrast between an animal surging away and the camel fixed in place, though wealth is absent.
terra: The donkeys flee from a predator, completing the motion image of 74:50; the link is limited to the section's animal movement contrast.

luna: The section's love is attachment to what seems good; this ayah names the preference beneath it as love of the immediate life (“تُحِبُّونَ الْعَاجِلَةَ”). | terra: بَلْ تُحِبُّونَ ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ generalizes the section's attaching love into love of the immediately available life.

luna: The next ayah completes the contrast begun in 75:20 by saying people leave the Hereafter (“وَتَذَرُونَ الْآخِرَةَ”), the horizon against which the section's hoarding is judged. | terra: وَتَذَرُونَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ states what that immediate attachment leaves behind, completing the preference named in 75:20.
terra: The righteous drink from a cup before the passage praises their feeding of loved food, so the vessel belongs to the same open-table sequence as 76:8.

luna: The section sets a shared meal against the Kenud who “eats alone”; this ayah has people give food to the needy, orphan, and captive while it is still loved (“عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ”), reversing the closed hand. | terra: They feed food to the poor, orphan, and captive despite loving it; love is present, but it moves the treasured thing outward rather than fastening the hand to it.

luna: After the people feed the needy and captive in 76:8, this ayah gives their stated motive: they feed solely for God (“لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ”), wanting neither repayment nor thanks, unlike the wealth-lover's self-serving grip.
luna: The feeders in 76:8–9 say they fear a stern day (“نَخَافُ ... يَوْمًا عَبُوسًا”); this ayah supplies that motive, linking generosity with the section's resurrection reckoning.
terra: Silver vessels and cups are circulated around the righteous in the same passage that praises them for feeding loved food in 76:8.
terra: Those who love the immediate life leave a heavy day behind them, opposing short possession to the reckoning that exposes attachment.
luna: When the records are spread (“الصُّحُفُ نُشِرَتْ”), this ayah gives another disclosure scene beside the section's gathered chest; 81:14 says each soul then knows what it brought.
luna: This ayah says every soul will know what it has brought (“مَا أَحْضَرَتْ”), making the deeds disclosed in 81:10 personal, as the section makes chest-contents answerable.
luna: This ayah says the graves are scattered (“بُعْثِرَتْ”), echoing the resurrection scene beside the section; 82:5 completes it by saying each soul knows what it sent ahead and left behind.
luna: After the graves scatter in 82:4, this ayah says each soul learns what it sent ahead and left behind (“قَدَّمَتْ وَأَخَّرَتْ”), making stored deeds answerable.

luna: The section's communal meal implies portions shared; this opening warning condemns short measure (“الْمُطَفِّفِينَ”), a reversal in which the giver of a portion cheats the receiver. | terra: Woe is pronounced upon those who take full measure for themselves; 83:2-3 show the one-way distribution that makes their receiving hand open and giving hand tight.

luna: This ayah specifies that the short-measure takers demand full measure when receiving (“اكْتَالُوا عَلَى النَّاسِ”), the self-favoring share-taking that the section's common table resists. | terra: When receiving by measure from others, the defrauders demand the full amount, specifying the acquisitive half of an unjust common transaction.

luna: The counterpart in this ayah is cheating people when weighing or measuring for them (“يُخْسِرُونَ”), completing the reversal of fair, divided provision. | terra: When measuring or weighing for others, they diminish the portion, the distributive opposite of the section's fairly divided common food.

luna: The section turns the clenched hand into a person whose inner contents are gathered; “يَوْمَ تُبْلَى السَّرَائِرُ” likewise makes concealed inner realities manifest on the Day of reckoning. | terra: On the day تُبْلَى ٱلسَّرَائِرُ, inner secrets are tested and exposed, a direct parallel to the section's gathered contents of the breasts.

luna: The section's collector attaches himself to immediate wealth before the final disclosure; this ayah names preferring the nearer life (“تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا”). | terra: Preferring the nearer life is the broad choice enacted in the section's attachment to stored wealth; 87:17 names what is better and lasting.

luna: Against the section's apparent “خَيْر” of riches, this ayah calls the Hereafter better (“خَيْرٌ”) and more lasting (“أَبْقَىٰ”). | terra: The Hereafter is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, using khayr for what is better and enduring rather than for the property preferred in 87:16.

luna: The section's table opposes solitary eating; this ayah indicts the failure to honor the orphan (“لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ”), naming one person the hoarder's closed hand leaves out. | terra: Refusing to honor the orphan identifies one recipient excluded by the hand that keeps wealth; 89:18-20 complete the linked food-and-wealth scene.

luna: The section puts a common pot and ladle against withheld help; this ayah asks why people do not urge one another to feed the poor (“طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ”). | terra: Failure to urge one another to feed the poor supplies the withheld communal meal immediately before the passage's indictment of consuming inheritance and loving wealth.

luna: After neglecting the orphan and hungry, this passage says “تَأْكُلُونَ التُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَّمًّا”: consuming inheritance greedily reverses the section's meal prepared for guests and shared out. | terra: Between failure to feed in 89:18 and love of wealth in 89:20, وَتَأْكُلُونَ ٱلتُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَّمًّا depicts inheritance swallowed wholesale rather than apportioned.

luna: The section's root حبّ explains attachment that sticks; here people “تُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا,” a piled-up love of wealth, immediately beside neglect of others. | terra: The direct حبّ المال joins love to wealth just as the section reads 100:8, and حُبًّا جَمًّا makes that attachment abundant and massed.

luna: After the passage's rebuke of neglecting the orphan and poor and loving wealth (89:17–20), this ayah voices regret: “يَا لَيْتَنِي قَدَّمْتُ لِحَيَاتِي”; it names what the hoarder wishes he had sent ahead.
terra: Freeing a neck begins the steep path whose next act is feeding in famine, reversing both the section's bound neck and abused dependent.
terra: Feeding on a day of hunger supplies the shared meal, while 90:15-16 identify the vulnerable diners.
terra: The orphan relative is one concrete recipient at the famine meal of 90:14, opposed to the solitary eater's exclusion of dependents.
terra: The destitute person in dust is the second named recipient at that meal, carrying the section's common food to one with nothing.

luna: The section depicts clinging love of wealth; this begins the other path with giving (“أَعْطَىٰ”) and God-consciousness, directly reversing the tight hand. | terra: The one who gives and is mindful begins the opposite path to the miser of 92:8, making release rather than self-sufficiency the easy course.
luna: The promise following the giving in 92:5–6 is that God will ease the giver toward ease (“فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ”), a reward against the collector's imagined security.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss of شديد is بخيل; this ayah uses “بَخِلَ” for the direct opposite of the giver in 92:5, the closed hand at the section's shared table. | terra: The one who is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient is the section's closed hand stated as a moral type.
luna: The consequence for the withholding path of 92:8–9 is ease toward hardship (“فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ”), reversing the promise of ease to the giver in 92:7.

luna: This ayah completes the withholding path: when the miser falls, his wealth (“مَالُهُ”) will not avail him, unlike the security he sought by keeping it. | terra: His wealth will not avail when he falls, overturning the collector's assumption that retained property can secure him.
terra: The person who gives his wealth to purify himself is the open-handed counterpart to the self-satisfied miser later contrasted within the surah.
terra: The command not to oppress the orphan directly reverses the kenud's treatment of a powerless dependent.
terra: The command not to repel the petitioner keeps the hand and table open to the person seeking help.
terra: The human being transgresses; 96:7 identifies the perception of self-sufficiency that makes abundance morally dangerous.
terra: أَن رَّءَاهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ names seeing oneself as self-sufficient, the inward judgment by which held wealth masters its holder.
terra: Competitive increase distracts people, a concise statement of the multiplying and counting impulse embodied by the section's collector.
terra: Competitive accumulation continues until people visit the graves, linking wealth's distraction to the graves opened in surah 100.

luna: The section's root جمع is gathering things together; this ayah names the person who “جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ,” accumulating wealth and repeatedly counting it. | terra: The person who جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ embodies the section's clenched collector: wealth is gathered and repeatedly counted rather than shared.
luna: The section turns the collector's hand toward the final reckoning; here the collector falsely supposes that his wealth (“مَالَهُ”) will make him last forever (“أَخْلَدَهُ”).
terra: The wealth-counter will be cast into the Crusher, beginning the reversal by which accumulated property fails to preserve the accumulator.
terra: The fire that follows the wealth-counter rises over the hearts, bringing punishment to the inner place whose contents the section says will be brought out.
terra: The fire is closed over the wealth-counter; the one who enclosed property is finally himself enclosed.
luna: The section's description of the Kenud includes beating a dependent and withholding aid; this ayah depicts the person who rudely repels the orphan (“يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ”).

luna: The section places a shared meal opposite solitary eating; here the condemned person does not encourage feeding the poor (“وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ”). | terra: The one who does not urge feeding the poor supplies the food-specific act behind the withholding of small aid in 107:7.

luna: The section's Kenud “withholds his help”; this ayah says they withhold even the small customary aid (“وَيَمْنَعُونَ الْمَاعُونَ”). | terra: وَيَمْنَعُونَ ٱلْمَاعُونَ names withholding even ordinary shared aid, the direct opposite of the section's utensils and common food.
terra: The declaration that neither a man's wealth nor his earnings avail him gives the same verdict against wealth imagined as protection or permanence.
